newsitem.title: UK: PRESS DIGEST - British business press - March 12.
newsitem.headline: PRESS DIGEST - British business press - March 12.

text.p: Prepared for Reuters by The Broadcast Monitoring Company
DAILY TELEGRAPH
- TOP PAY BONANZA AT LLOYDS TSB

Newly created banking group Lloyds TSB spent more than five million stg last year on bumper salary and bonus packages to directors and several payments to former directors of TSB TSB.L and merchant bank Hill Samuel. The payments came at the end of a record first year for the group, which produced a 52 per cent leap in pre-tax profits, and marked a change in the fortunes of many directors.
- REDROW HEAD TO NET 91 MILLION STG IN SHARE SALE

Founder and chairman of housebuilder Redrow, Steve Morgan, is set to sell 24 percent of the company's shares. This will net him a windfall of up to 91 million stg. He refuted speculation that he was selling to raise funds to increase his holding in Liverpool Football Club, in which he already owns a five per cent stake. He said the sale was being held on the advice of institutions and he had not decided what to do with the proceeds.
-AMSTRAD TAPS THE MARKET FOR 'WORLD TELEPHONE'

Electronics group run by Alan Sugar, Amstrad, looks set to launch a phone which will allow mobile phones to be used anywhere in the world. Amstrad subsidiary Dancall will launch the first mobile phone able to switch automatically between the different frequencies used in America and those used throughout Europe and the Middle East at a trade show in Hanover. The new phone will be in the shops by Christmas and will fetch a premium of up to ten per cent on existing hand sets.
THE TIMES
- HOPKINS 'NOT FIT TO BE DIRECTOR'

The Securities and Futures Authority, the regulator for brokers and futures traders, has declared that Ian Hopkins, the former head of group treasury and risk at Barings, had "ceased to be a fit and proper person to be registered with the SFA as a director". This is one of the stiffest penalties yet on a Barings executive charged with supervising Nick Leeson's rogue trades on the Far East money markets.
- NATWEST SET TO CUT BONUS PAYMENTS AFTER INQUIRY

The conclusion of the NatWest inquiry, conducted by accountants Coopers and Lybrand and City law firm Linklaters and Paines, has led to senior managers responsible for supervising the derivatives trading of Kyriacos Papouis, which led to the bank writing-off 50 million stg, having their bonuses cut. The inquiry will lead to the departure of a number of senior managers in the interest rate options department at NatWest Markets.
- ZENECA TO EXPAND US SALESFORCE AS PROFITS TOP ONE BILLION STG

To support the launch of Zeneca's strong portfolio of new drugs in the healthcare market the pharmaceutical group is set to expand its US salesforce from 1,200 to 2,000. Zeneca said that products launched within the last two years were responsible for 40 per cent of the volume growth in pharmaceutical last year and were responsible for five per cent of the division's 2.4 billion stg of sales.
THE GUARDIAN
- ALUMINUM 'CZAR' ACCUSED
David Reuben, who has been called the 'czar' of the world aluminum market, has been accused of dooming the local aluminum trade to poverty by Russian interior minister Anatoly Kulikov.

Reuben controls two-thirds of Russia's aluminum production through his company Trans-World. He is opposing threats from the Russians to renationalise the industry. If the Russians are successful it is likely that less of the country's aluminum output would be traded on the world's market, massively increasing prices.
- PIA MIS-SELLING HUNT IS FRUITLESS

It has been revealed that the Personal Investment Authority has one of the worst records in securing redress for victims. This comes after the City watchdog was reprimanded by MPs for its handling of the pensions mis-selling review. The news contradicts comments made by PIA chief executive, Colette Bowe, to the Treasury select committee that the insurance industry alone was responsible for carrying out the review of mis-sold personal pensions.
